overlap.title: The purification periods differ by the child’s sex

overlap.title: Burning and eating depend on the offering category
overlap.summary: The rules distinguish altar portions, priestly food and offerings that must be burned.
overlap.reasoning: The chapter 6 exceptions explain why a command to eat one offering need not conflict with a command to burn another. Offering type, priestly ownership and blood destination matter.
overlap.scope: This compares stated ritual categories, not every later legal interpretation, historical practice or ethical issue concerning animal sacrifice.

overlap.title: Unrecognized wrongdoing can still require atonement
overlap.summary: The laws distinguish not knowing about an offense from learning of it and responding.
overlap.reasoning: Lack of knowledge does not simply erase responsibility in these rules. Their specified remedies should not automatically be generalized to every deliberate offense.
overlap.scope: This describes the law’s framing, not a modern judgment of culpability, evidence of uniform enforcement or a comprehensive theory of forgiveness.

overlap.title: Ignorance and presumptuous defiance receive different remedies
overlap.summary: The chapter provides atonement for inadvertent offenses but prescribes exclusion for presumptuous wrongdoing.
overlap.reasoning: A summary that every offense is remedied simply by an offering omits the express contrast. The individual and community procedures also should not be conflated.
overlap.scope: This describes the stated categories, not a complete taxonomy of all offenses or proof of historical enforcement. Exact legal terminology and comparison with other collections remain open.
